texts: What belongs in the note for a CNShopper manual purchase?

Include the seller URL, original option text, size, colour and quantity. If the seller offers a set and separate pieces, name the piece you want. State whether you want to be contacted if the exact option is unavailable.
How do I order two colours of the same item without mixing them up?

Record each colour as a separate line with its size and count. For example, two navy medium shirts and one grey large shirt are two distinct selections. Compare both lines with the purchase confirmation.
Can I identify a seller listing using only a screenshot?

Use the screenshot to find candidates, then compare seller, item number and available options. A copied studio picture can appear in several shops. Save the seller URL before submitting a purchase request.
What if a translated option sounds like the wrong product?

Keep the original option text and screenshot the selected swatch. Ask what that exact option includes before paying. A price for a cushion cover, for example, can appear next to a photograph of a filled cushion.
What should I do if a 1688 offer has a minimum quantity?

Check the seller’s minimum, whether different colours can be combined and the price tier for your total. Ask CNShopper to confirm the requested mix if the imported order does not display those conditions clearly.
How can I check whether a Chinese size chart fits me?

Look at the measurement diagram and units. Compare a similar garment you own using the same endpoints. If the chart gives a flat width and your notes give a circumference, convert the units and measurement method before choosing a size.
When does international freight enter my CNShopper budget?

Allow for it before the purchase. CNShopper describes collecting the product payment first and calculating international shipping after warehouse measurement. Leave room for a parcel quote based on the actual contents.
How should I record delivery charges from several sellers?
Record domestic delivery on each seller order and outbound freight on the parcel record. If two items share one domestic charge, enter it once. Keep the currency alongside each amount.
The seller says delivered. Where should I look for my purchase?

Check the destination on that tracking record. A domestic delivery to the CNShopper warehouse precedes the outbound parcel. Match the seller tracking number to the order and check the warehouse record before looking for an international scan.
How do I check a delivery containing only part of an order?

Make a list of expected pieces and mark the items identifiable in the warehouse entry. Compare seller tracking numbers for a second shipment. Give support the order reference and identify the pieces still unaccounted for.
Which warehouse photo would help confirm a personalised print?

Request a view showing the entire printed area and another close enough to read the lettering. Compare spelling, number and placement against your written order before packing. Keep the original text with the photos.
What should I do if the warehouse image shows the wrong size label?

Save the image and the order confirmation showing the selected size. Point out the two labels in your message and ask for a check before international shipment. A measurement can help if two labels use different sizing systems.
What should I check before combining orders into one parcel?

Confirm each item has arrived, completed any inspection you need and is eligible for the intended route. Compare one combined quote with separate quotes using the same destination and packing assumptions.
Which measurements matter when I compare parcel estimates?

Write down packed length, width, height and actual weight, with units. Keep destination and route constant when testing how a packing decision changes the estimate. Record any service included in only one quote.
How can I tell if an after-sales case concerns the seller or the carrier?

Identify when the issue first appeared. A wrong colour in a warehouse image points to the item order. Damage first observed on delivery also calls for parcel-label, packaging and delivery evidence. Provide both references if the cause is uncertain.
Where should I look for CNShopper’s current order and return instructions?

The official How to Order guide describes purchasing and parcel submission. The official FAQ links to After-Sales & Returns and the warehouse policy. Check those pages and the specific order before acting on an older screenshot.
Which CNShopper order number belongs with a payment receipt?
Use the purchase or parcel reference attached to the payment, and note which stage it covers. Save the payment provider's transaction reference separately so support can match both systems.
Should I ask the seller to substitute a different shade if mine is unavailable?
State your preference explicitly. If shade matters, ask to be contacted before substitution and keep the original seller colour text with the request.
Can a listed measurement tell me whether trousers will fit over my shoes?
Compare the leg opening, inseam and rise separately with trousers you already wear. Confirm whether the seller measured the opening flat or around its circumference before comparing numbers.
How should I identify an order when two similar parcels arrive?
Match each external label to its outbound tracking number before unpacking. Photograph the contents of one parcel at a time and record the linked warehouse entries.
What if the seller changes the price before the purchase is confirmed?
Compare the revised amount with your original option, quantity and domestic shipping. Ask what changed and decide whether to accept the revised total before authorizing a different purchase.
Comparing CNShopper shipping estimates for two destinations

Two people want the same purchase delivered to different addresses. A quote for one destination cannot tell you what the second person will pay. Available routes, address requirements and services can differ even if the parcel never changes shape. Build a controlled comparison first, then decide whether any difference comes from the destination, the parcel or the choices attached to the route.
Define what you need the comparison to answer

Are you deciding where to send one parcel, or comparing the cost of two separate shipments? Those are different questions. Sending one complete parcel to address A or address B changes only the destination if every other input stays constant. Sending half the goods to each address creates two new parcels with different contents, dimensions and possibly different packing requirements.

Suppose a buyer can receive a parcel at home or while staying with family abroad. The initial comparison can use the same goods and packing for both endpoints. If the buyer also considers sending a gift separately to a relative, treat that as a third scenario. Mixing a complete parcel to one country with a smaller gift parcel to another does not isolate the effect of destination.
Create a parcel description that can be repeated

Record the included warehouse entries, product types, quantities, outer dimensions and actual or estimated packed weight. Mark the packing state explicitly. Are retail boxes retained? Is a fragile item protected? Have the items actually been measured together, or are you working from seller dimensions? Use the same assumptions for both destination searches or identify each deliberate change.

Imagine one book, two folded shirts and a rigid pencil case. If the initial quote uses a carton measuring 35 by 25 by 15 centimetres at 1,800 grams, copy those values into the second comparison in the units requested. Do not enter the book dimensions for the second search by mistake. Preserve the figures as illustrative until they represent a real measured parcel. A consistent assumption makes a meaningful comparison even before the final quote is available.
Check the destination information required by the service

Enter the destination country or region accurately and provide the postcode or other address detail if the quote process asks for it. A city name can describe a wide service area. The route available for a major urban address may differ from the one available for a remote location. Check the live service information instead of inferring availability from the presence of a country's name in an example list.

Verify that the recipient can actually receive at the chosen address. An estimate is of little use if a particular service does not accept the address format, if a required delivery detail is missing or if the recipient will have left before the parcel can reasonably arrive. Keep sensitive details in the official service rather than a public comparison table. A private label such as “home” or “family address” is enough for your own side-by-side worksheet.
Compare the route conditions before comparing the number

For each destination, record the route name, estimated charge, currency, published delivery estimate and any included or optional services you care about. Read the conditions for your item types and parcel size. If a route is unavailable for one destination, mark it unavailable instead of treating a blank result as a zero price. Consider other eligible services, but identify when you are comparing different routes.

A route with a lower displayed amount may use a different handoff, delivery method or service level. That can be acceptable if it satisfies your actual requirements. A time-sensitive gift and ordinary household supplies may justify different trade-offs. Identify which condition matters before choosing the lowest row in the table. An estimated transit window should be recorded as an estimate and interpreted alongside the current terms, not as a promise for a particular delivery date.
Keep currencies and included services consistent

Record the original quote currency and use a clearly dated conversion for a rough comparison if needed. Check whether each figure includes the same optional treatment. An estimate that includes reinforcement and one that omits it can both be accurate while answering different questions. If the same protection is required for both destinations, add it consistently where the service permits or mark the missing price as unknown.

For a numerical illustration, suppose one quote shows 85 units of your comparison currency for freight plus 5 for required packing, while the second shows 92 including the same packing. The comparable amounts are 90 and 92. Comparing 85 and 92 exaggerates the difference. If the second quote does not state whether packing is included, leave that total unresolved until you can verify it. These numbers explain the arithmetic and do not represent a CNShopper rate.
Separate a destination comparison from a split-parcel decision

If the real alternative is sending two parcels, obtain estimates for both proposed parcels. Write down which items each contains and how each will be packed. One bulky item can determine most of the external size of a mixed parcel, while a second small parcel can still incur its own service charge. Dividing the combined box's dimensions or price in half does not produce two reliable quotes.

Take the example with a book, shirts and pencil case. One possible arrangement sends all four pieces to address A. Another sends the book to address B and the shirts and case to address A. The second arrangement has two service decisions and two actual delivery events. Add both eligible quotes and relevant packing amounts before comparing the total with the single-parcel alternative. Also consider what the intended recipients actually need; the lowest combined quote may deliver the wrong item to one of them.
Record what the quote can and cannot settle

A shipping estimate can help compare route options for the supplied inputs. It cannot guarantee that measurements will stay unchanged after packing or determine every possible destination charge. Consult the current route description, destination requirements and applicable official guidance for issues specific to the delivery. Avoid borrowing a tax percentage, fixed threshold or delivery promise from an unrelated country's spreadsheet.

CNShopper's ordering guide places international shipping after warehouse receipt and parcel preparation. Use the early comparison to decide whether a purchase still fits a realistic budget. Recheck when the actual warehouse measurements and final address are available. If a route disappears at that stage, compare the remaining eligible options instead of assuming the original line ought to be available at the old price.
Preserve the decision with its assumptions

Save the pair of quotes, date, parcel description and choice in a private record. Name the factor that determined the outcome. For instance, “same packed carton, different destinations; chose address B because the eligible service fit the recipient's schedule and total budget.” If the choice depended on an estimated weight, mark it for review after the actual packing data arrives.

A later change in price is easier to understand if you can identify which input moved. Perhaps the destination stayed the same but the carton expanded after protection was added. Perhaps the box stayed the same but the service selected in the new quote differs. A clear comparison does more than rank two numbers. It gives you a repeatable way to make a destination decision with the parcel you will actually send.

Preserve the assumptions with the quote you choose. When the actual parcel is packed, update its weight and dimensions and check the service still offered for the complete address. This last check is particularly important if the two addresses had different delivery arrangements. A parcel that looked cheaper to send to a relative may become less attractive if its size prevents collection from the intended location.
CNShopper spreadsheet search: when to use a product link and when a photo helps

If you have the seller's original product link, start there. If you have only a picture, image search can lead you to candidate listings. The evidence required to identify the original changes with the starting point. A product identifier can link two records on the same marketplace. A visually similar image helps narrow a search, but it cannot tell you which seller posted a photograph first or which option a buyer selected.
Decide what you are trying to recover

There are two useful search goals. You may want the very same seller listing because you need a compatible replacement piece or want to check a previous order. Alternatively, you may simply want a product with a similar appearance. Write down which goal applies. A result that is excellent for visual inspiration may be insufficient for replacing a specific component.

Suppose your picture shows a transparent desk drawer with a distinctive curved handle. If you just want a similar organiser, several matching shapes may be worth comparing. If you need another drawer to fit an existing frame, exact external width, rail spacing and depth are decisive. In the second case, the photograph is the beginning of identification rather than enough evidence to place the order.
Use a source link when one exists

Open the marketplace link and record the seller, item identifier and option text. Check whether the page still offers the relevant combination. CNShopper's ordering guide describes submitting a product link with size, colour, quantity and other purchase details. A saved link makes a strong starting point, yet it can still point to a listing whose available variants have changed since you first saw it.

If your saved address opens a share landing page, navigate to the product and compare its final identity. If it opens a shop, search result or expired offer, do not treat the generic page as the original product. Look for the identifier in the original receipt, seller conversation or page title if available. Keep the marketplace with the number; identical-looking numbers drawn from different services are not automatically comparable.
Prepare a photo that contains useful evidence

Crop a search image to one main object while retaining enough of its shape to distinguish it. A close crop of an ordinary metal zip can return many unrelated products. A wider view showing the zip position, unusual pocket and overall outline gives the search more relevant features. Save the uncropped original because it may contain details needed later even if they distract from the initial search.

Try another angle when the first image is dominated by a generic printed graphic or background. For the drawer, a front view may show the curved handle while a side view reveals the rail profile. Those two views answer different questions. Keep track of which image produced which candidate rather than assuming that a similar first result under both searches proves a common source.
Compare structure before colour

Look for features that remain recognizable under different lighting: screw positions, number of pockets, spacing of openings, seam direction, underside features or the shape of a hinge. Colour alone can vary with white balance, editing and screen settings. Use visible differences to rule out candidates first; one incompatible structural detail may matter more than five generic similarities.

Imagine two transparent drawers shown at different angles. Both have a curved handle and the same general outline. One uses a single central rail, while the other has two side rails. If your existing frame requires the twin-rail version, the single-rail candidate is unsuitable regardless of how close its colour appears. Mark that reason in your shortlist. It prevents the same appealing but incompatible result from re-entering the decision during a later search.
Treat reused photographs as weak evidence of identity

Multiple sellers can display the same promotional photograph. The fact that the images match exactly may say more about the image source than the physical stock. Open each candidate listing and compare the seller identity, available variants, dimensions, package contents and current order terms. If a product has seller-specific or warehouse photographs, use them to examine the details the promotional view leaves uncertain.

Avoid claiming an item is genuine, identical in material or made by a particular manufacturer because two images match. Image search compares visible appearance. It cannot establish the underlying supply chain, a product's functional performance or which unit the merchant will dispatch. If those facts matter, seek evidence appropriate to the question and choose whether the remaining uncertainty is acceptable.
Confirm the selected variant independently

A correct listing can still produce the wrong item. Once you have identified a candidate, select the exact size, colour and package option and see whether the image or price changes. Save the original option wording with your notes. An organiser listing might combine a frame, a spare drawer and a complete unit. The picture showing a finished organiser does not establish that all three options include the frame.

For a replacement purchase, write a compatibility specification. Record the measurements and connection details from your existing item using named endpoints. Compare those with the actual seller information. If the seller measures the inside width while you need the outside width at the rails, the numbers are not directly comparable. Ask the seller or agent to clarify the specific dimension instead of treating a visually convincing match as proof that the part will fit.
Build a shortlist that shows what remains unknown

Use a small table or note with four fields: candidate source link, features that match, features that contradict and facts still needed. A candidate with no visible contradiction may still lack the one measurement that controls fit. Keeping unknowns separate from matches makes the decision clearer. It also helps you phrase a question that someone can answer without reviewing your entire search history.

For example, candidate A may match the handle and two rails but lack a width measurement. Candidate B may have a confirmed width and an incompatible single rail. Candidate C may use the exact promotional picture but offer no usable option details. The next useful action is to ask about candidate A's external width. Searching for another dozen indistinguishable front photographs is unlikely to resolve that particular uncertainty.
Connect the eventual order to the evidence

When you select a listing, save the actual seller page, chosen option, required measurement and purchase reference. At warehouse intake, check the feature that made the candidate acceptable. If fit depended on twin rails, a front picture alone cannot confirm them. Ask what inspection options are available and request a view showing the relevant location, keeping the image associated with the correct warehouse entry.

Finally, record whether you recovered the original listing or selected a visually similar alternative. Both can be sensible outcomes. A replacement part benefits from a stronger identity and measurement chain; an aesthetic shortlist can tolerate more variation. Being explicit about the outcome prevents a helpful search result from becoming an unsupported guarantee about a seller, variant or product that the photograph could never establish.

If your search started with a picture of an item you already own, measure the feature that makes it useful to you. A replacement pouch might need to fit an existing insert, or a cover might need openings in a particular position. Record that dimension or layout before browsing visually similar models. When you narrow the results to two listings, compare how clearly each seller documents that requirement. A slightly less similar photograph can lead to the better-supported choice if its details answer the practical question that motivated the search.
CNShopper link import or manual order: deciding what to do when a listing fails

You paste a seller link into a shopping agent and the item does not appear as expected. Sometimes the source page has disappeared. Sometimes the page exists but the agent cannot capture an important option. Sometimes the wrong link was copied. A manual order is useful when a purchaser can identify a real offer from the information you provide. It does not repair an offer that you cannot identify yourself.
Check whether the link is a product page

Open the original marketplace link and inspect its destination. Does it show one product with a seller and options? A search-results page, seller homepage, promotional album or social-media photograph can contain the item without identifying a purchasable listing. Copy the product page rather than the page that led you to it. Preserve the marketplace name and item identifier if visible.

Imagine saving a screenshot of a desk organiser from a seller's gallery. Tapping the shared address opens the shop's entire stationery collection. You can recognize the product in a picture, but the purchaser still needs to know which listing and option to buy. Find the individual organiser or ask the seller for its link. A manual note that says “third item in the picture” may become unusable when the seller changes the display order.
Understand what a successful import should establish

CNShopper's ordering guide describes starting with a marketplace link and confirming the item, option, quantity and cost before purchase. Use that sequence to test the import. Match the seller, item identity, variant choices and price for the actual option you want. A page loading successfully is only the first result. If the cheapest option is an accessory while you want the complete product, the price beside the first picture does not settle the purchase.

Try making the complete selection before deciding that something is missing. A size list may depend on the colour you chose first. A bundle may expose another selector for its contents. After all fields are set, read the final summary together. If it faithfully describes your intended item, a normal link-based order provides a simpler record than re-entering the same information manually.
Distinguish an import problem from a seller problem

Return to the seller page and check whether the combination exists there. If the seller offers green in medium but the imported page omits that option, you have an identifiable discrepancy to ask about. If the seller no longer lists green at all, a manual order cannot establish that the seller has one. Ask about availability before authorizing payment or selecting another colour.

For an edited listing, keep the date of your evidence. A screenshot from last month may explain what you were seeking but may no longer describe the current offer. Save the current seller page alongside the older reference and identify the difference. For example, “the older page displayed a detachable tray; today's option only names the organiser body.” A clear question about the tray is more useful than resubmitting an old link and hoping it restores the former bundle.
Build a manual request from positive identifiers

If a manual or DIY purchase is offered for your case, state the seller URL, product name, exact original option text, intended colour, size, unit and quantity. Add the price as displayed for that selection and specify its currency. Include a screenshot of the selected option where it resolves ambiguity. The request should allow the purchaser to find the offer even if the translation of its title changes.

Separate instructions from questions. “Buy the 36-centimetre grey organiser with removable tray, quantity one, if the tray is included in this option” is a conditional instruction. “Can the seller confirm that the tray is included?” is the question that must be answered first. If the condition matters to you, state whether you want the purchase held until you receive an answer. Avoid choosing a cheaper option and writing the name of a different product in the notes.
Keep substitutions under your control

A manual request sometimes becomes ambiguous when a seller cannot supply the exact selection. Decide in advance which differences are acceptable. Some buyers would accept a different outer carton but insist on the same dimensions. Others need an exact shade for a matching set. State the requirement and what the purchaser should do if it cannot be met.

An example is a pair of matching storage boxes. The blue shade shown in your reference matches an existing shelf, while a seller also offers teal. The two option pictures look alike on a phone but the seller names differ. If colour determines the purchase, write “please ask before replacing the selected blue with another shade.” Do not write “anything similar is fine” merely to complete the form unless that is truly your decision.
Verify the commercial details before paying

For a manual selection, compare the confirmed product price, unit count and domestic delivery with the original seller offer. If the figure changes, identify why. It may reflect a higher-priced variant, a minimum order, shipping from the seller or a newer price. An explanation that aligns the order with the actual listing lets you make a purchasing decision. A guessed reason does not.

Consider a listed amount of 30 for a replacement lid and 110 for the complete container. If you request the full container, the difference is not an unexplained surcharge. Conversely, if the confirmed amount is 110 for a lid-only option, that discrepancy needs clarification. Use illustrative figures only to understand the distinction. Your actual order should retain the seller's current amount and currency, and the international parcel budget should remain separate from the purchase payment.
Decide when to stop and look elsewhere

If neither the listing nor the seller can identify the requested option, pause rather than converting uncertainty into an order. A manual form can communicate an intention; it cannot supply missing evidence about availability, authorization to sell or exactly what is included. If you choose an alternative seller, begin a new comparison. Do not carry over the previous seller's size table, expected accessories or photographs as if they describe the replacement.

In some cases a direct source link returns after a seller updates the page or sends a corrected address. Recheck the new link against your requirements and decide whether link import now provides a complete offer. If an earlier manual request is still open, identify it and avoid telling two purchasers to buy the same unit. Confirm which request will proceed before paying twice or cancelling the wrong record.
Carry the selection through warehouse review

Once the order is confirmed, keep your final specification with the order reference. At warehouse intake, use that specification to review the actual item. A photograph showing one grey organiser may establish its colour and general shape, while a view of the lid and tray laid out together may be necessary to confirm the bundle. Ask about the unresolved feature while the item is still accessible for inspection.

The practical test is whether your order can be read by someone who never saw the original shortlist. They should be able to name the seller, identify the product, reproduce the option, count the units and say what to do if a key feature is unavailable. When link import supplies that information, use it. When only a manual request can carry it accurately, give the purchaser a specification they can verify. The workflow should follow the quality of the offer you actually found.

If the original listing later begins importing correctly, check your purchase history before starting over. A manually submitted request and a new imported cart line can both refer to the same desired unit. Mark which request should proceed and resolve the other through the order's available controls.
One CNShopper order arrived in part: working out which units are still missing

A warehouse picture showing one product does not automatically mean the seller sent only one. Other pieces might be in a second domestic parcel, inside the same carton, listed under a different warehouse entry or absent from the shipment. Establish the expected contents and the evidence for each physical delivery before deciding which question belongs with the seller and which belongs with the warehouse.
Start with what you actually ordered

Open the accepted purchase record. Identify each option and its ordered quantity, then list the physical components included in each option. The same product photograph can illustrate a full set and separate pieces. If you bought “top only,” a missing pair of trousers is not a warehouse shortage even when the seller's main picture displays a complete outfit.

Consider a stationery order containing two pencil cases and one refill kit. The kit includes three refills according to the paid option. Your purchase therefore has three ordered units and five principal physical pieces. A seller might pack the refills inside one pencil case, place them in a separate sleeve or send them later. Keep the expected physical count alongside the order units so that a warehouse entry stating one kit can be interpreted correctly.
Ask what the seller dispatched under each number

Find each domestic carrier number associated with the purchase. A seller order can generate more than one waybill if stock is split between locations or dispatched at different times. A replacement label can also create a second number without a second physical parcel. Look for collection and movement events, and ask the seller which numbers were actually used when the record is unclear.

Write a line for each waybill with the carrier, latest event and contents the seller says it contains. Leave the contents unknown if the seller has not confirmed them. A small parcel's weight cannot establish that it contains the refills rather than one empty pencil case. Guessing the allocation may seem efficient until the guesses conflict with the warehouse pictures and send the investigation toward the wrong box.
Give each stage its own status

CNShopper's tracking guide describes seller dispatch, warehouse arrival, matching to an order, inspection and subsequent international delivery as separate stages. A carrier can report a delivery before you can identify its stocked goods. Conversely, an item in the warehouse can be ready for review while another carton from the same purchase remains in transit. Mark those states independently.

For the stationery example, suppose waybill A shows delivery and a warehouse image clearly shows one pencil case. Waybill B shows collection without delivery. You can say one case is visually accounted for and another domestic parcel is moving. You cannot yet conclude that one case and a refill kit were lost. The next useful question is what seller B's carton contains and whether the first case has any smaller pieces packed inside.
Inspect the right entry without overinterpreting a photograph

Match the warehouse reference, option label, colour and count with the expected pieces. Inspect the entire photo group when available. A photograph of a closed container establishes little about accessories inside. A picture showing an open pencil case and wrapped refills can support a count if the pieces are visible enough to distinguish. Describe exactly what the image confirms.

If the critical part is hidden, request a targeted check subject to available services. “For the navy pencil case on entry X, please check whether the separately ordered refill kit is inside the zipped pocket” is specific. A request for a new front view of the closed case will probably repeat information you already have. State whether opening sealed retail packaging is acceptable before assuming staff can expose every part.
Distinguish three common discrepancies

The first is a timing difference: one of several known parcels has not arrived. Continue tracking that specific carrier number. The second is an identity difference: the parcel arrived but the warehouse description or reference is hard to match. Provide the seller and carrier evidence to CNShopper. The third is a contents difference: the relevant carton is identified, but a purchased component is absent from the recorded contents. Ask for a contents check and compare it with the merchant's packing statement.

These outcomes can coexist. The first box might contain the correct pencil case but the wrong colour, while the second is still in transit. Record the visible colour problem separately from the missing-arrival question. Solving one will not solve the other. If you report the whole order as simply incomplete, support may answer the carrier question and miss the fact that a visible item could require action before dispatch.
Decide whether partial dispatch serves your purpose

After identifying the arrived units, decide whether you need them together. Two independent gifts can be useful on different timelines. A case ordered specifically to hold the missing tools may be unsuitable to send without them. Consider any relevant seller remedy, warehouse storage conditions, packing requirements and actual parcel options before selecting the available entries for international delivery.

Compare the full alternatives. One quote for the current pieces does not represent the cost of shipping the later pieces separately. A future combined quote may also change when all dimensions are known. Record the chosen scenario as “dispatch confirmed item now; remaining items held for intake” or “wait for all matched pieces.” That wording prevents a later reader from assuming every item on the original purchase was inside the first outbound parcel.
Assemble a small exception message

Start with the order reference and a one-sentence description of what was purchased. Add the relevant carrier number, current delivery event, warehouse entry and the exact unit still in question. Explain which units you have already matched. Attach the order confirmation and the image or merchant response that demonstrates the discrepancy. More screenshots are helpful only if each contributes a different fact.

An example is: “The order was for two cases and one three-piece refill kit. One case is visible under entry X. The seller says the kit travelled under waybill A with that case, while the second case is on waybill B. Can you check whether the refill pouch was recorded inside entry X?” Add the actual references privately. This message asks the warehouse to verify a specific claim without asking it to explain a second carton that has not arrived.
Close the purchase by unit, then by parcel

When another warehouse entry appears, compare it with the outstanding list rather than restarting the investigation. If the second case arrives and its pocket contains the refills, update both the physical count and the seller's earlier packing assumption. Keep the correction dated. If the refills remain absent and all domestic cartons have been checked, you now have a more precise basis for an after-sales inquiry.

Finish by mapping every accepted unit to a warehouse reference and, later, to its outbound parcel. A product can be ordered, received, inspected and shipped on four different dates. Keeping those dates and counts separate allows you to say exactly where something is missing. It also keeps a normal split delivery from turning into an unnecessary claim while preserving the evidence you need if a shortage is real.

When you release the first items for shipping, save the exact list you selected. Later, the account may show a delivered international parcel alongside a newly arrived warehouse item from the same original purchase. A saved selection lets you recognize this as the outcome you chose. It also prevents you from reporting the later item as missing from a parcel that was never supposed to contain it.
How to read a CNShopper order timeline from purchase to delivery

An order timeline starts to make sense when you ask which object each update describes. A purchasing agent can buy several products on your behalf. A seller can send several boxes for one purchase. The warehouse can combine selected items into a new international parcel. The tracking events for those objects belong to different records. CNShopper's official ordering guide and tracking information describe the journey through purchase, warehouse and shipment. Use those stages to locate the last confirmed event for the particular item you care about.
Begin with the question the timeline needs to answer

Suppose you ordered a blue shirt and a folding bag. The shirt has appeared in your warehouse inventory and the bag still appears under orders. Your practical question is whether the bag has reached the warehouse. A delivery notification on your phone could belong to the shirt alone. Open the bag's purchase line and write down its seller, variant, quantity and order identifier. Follow any domestic tracking number attached to that line. Check whether the shirt has the same number before treating the notification as evidence about both items.

Write the last event as a full sentence with a subject. “The seller supplied a domestic shipment number for the bag” records exactly what you know. “It has shipped” leaves room for three interpretations, including that the agent sent your international parcel. Keep this discipline if you are asking someone else to check the status. A short sentence often gives a support agent more information than a screenshot in which the identifier, carrier and product line are offscreen.
Separate a successful payment from a completed purchase

A payment record tells you that a transaction took place in your account. Look at the individual purchase lines to find out whether the selected seller option was actually ordered. An agent might need clarification about a color, size, quantity or changed price. Read messages attached to the order even when the account balance and payment record look correct. If a reply is required, include the full option wording and specify what should happen if the seller no longer offers it.

Different lines in the same transaction can progress independently. Put the seller and order reference next to each line in your notes. Two identical-looking hats from different shops can have separate purchase histories, domestic shipments and warehouse entries. If one line gets canceled, save the associated notice and compare the amount and currency against the record of that specific purchase. The payment for the original basket can remain visible even after the individual lines have gone in different directions.
Follow domestic tracking to its endpoint

After the seller gives the shipment to a domestic carrier, the destination on that waybill is the receiving address in China. A carrier event showing delivery at that address marks the endpoint of the domestic journey. The next evidence you need comes from the receiving warehouse. Its staff must be able to associate a package with your purchase before you can inspect the corresponding item in your account. Look for a new warehouse entry and compare its photographs and quantity with the expected purchase.

If the domestic timeline has stopped, identify the last event and its issuer. A waybill created by a seller, a collection scan by the carrier and a delivery scan are different observations. Copy the exact text, displayed time and tracking number. Ask whether the seller gave the package to the carrier if collection is the open question. Ask the agent to check intake against the waybill if delivery was already recorded. This directs the inquiry to whoever can establish the next fact.
Read the warehouse record alongside the purchase

Inventory gives you a chance to confirm what arrived. Check the number of units and the options visible in the photographs. A photograph of a labeled sealed package may show a size code and still leave the contents unseen. Make a specific request if the missing observation determines whether you would keep the item. For example, ask for a clear view of the size label on the garment for the identified warehouse line. Check any service charge and whether the request is available before approving it.

If you asked for two units and see only one, inspect the purchase line and domestic waybills before merging anything. A second box may be traveling separately, or the missing unit may have been packed beside the first. State which possibilities remain open when you write to support. Preserve the original warehouse photos with the reference so that later packing and shipment updates do not make it difficult to explain what was visible at intake.
Switch to the international parcel reference

When you submit warehouse items for shipping, a new parcel can contain items from several purchases. Record the parcel reference next to the items you actually included. Items still in storage keep their warehouse records. If you subsequently add another order to your account, its appearance in the same account does not establish that it joined the submitted parcel. Use the saved parcel contents and packing information to identify which goods the outbound shipment represents.

A parcel submission or a paid freight charge can precede physical collection. Open the shipping record to find the chosen service and its tracking number when available. Consult that service's own tracking page for the movement associated with this leg. If the page has no event, verify that you copied the outbound number and that you selected the indicated service. Copying a domestic number into an international carrier's form is an easy way to turn a routine record mismatch into an apparent missing package.
Interpret a handover between carriers

Some services display a different tracking reference once a destination partner takes over. Search the shipment details for a named partner or linked number. Record where that information came from so you can connect the two histories later. Compare dates with the stated locations and time zones. An update processed in one country can appear in a different order from an update recorded locally, especially if the system imports several events together.

If the most recent event says delivery was attempted, inspect the carrier's actual notice for the next action and the address details it can display. A household member, reception desk or parcel locker may hold information the purchasing agent cannot see. Use official account pages or carrier websites to look up the parcel. When requesting a trace, give the tracking reference through the appropriate private support channel and keep personal address details out of public screenshots.
Close the timeline with an observable result

On receipt, compare the contents with the outbound packing record, then compare each item with its purchase and warehouse entry. This two-step comparison matters when you deliberately shipped only part of an order. If something is missing, identify the earliest record where the expected quantity and the observed quantity differ. An intake photograph showing two units and a packing record showing one points to a different question from a warehouse entry that always showed one.

Keep a short closing note with the relevant references, the observation and any unresolved action. A note that says “bag received, shirt remained in storage by choice” preserves a decision that a delivery scan could never capture. If the parcel has an issue, move the evidence to an after-sales request and ask one concrete question about the affected line. The timeline then does its most valuable job. It shows the next person exactly where a verified sequence ended and what remains to be checked.
Keeping the seller's option wording intact in a CNShopper order

Two options can look identical after translation even though the seller treats them as different products. A code, suffix or small drawing in the selector can distinguish size systems, bundle contents, revisions or finishes. Preserve enough of the original selection that a buyer can reproduce your choice. A readable English description helps explain your intention; the seller's exact wording helps identify the control that actually orders it.
Capture the selection rather than the product title

A product title generally describes the family of items. The option identifies which member of that family you want. Open the seller page, make the complete selection and save the exact wording beside the product link. If the option is a picture with little text, save a screenshot showing which swatch is highlighted and how it relates to the product.

Consider a notebook listing titled “A5 travel journal, multiple colours.” The title supplies almost no information about whether the selected pages are lined, dotted or blank. A thumbnail displaying a closed navy cover can represent all three. If the selector specifies a code such as B2, preserve that code exactly along with your reading of it. Do not assume B2 means blank unless the seller's own option key establishes the connection.
Keep the original and your interpretation in separate fields

When you translate a seller option, keep the source phrase visible beside your translation. A purchaser can then check whether your plain-language interpretation matches the actual button. This also allows you to correct an interpretation later without losing the only reliable record of the selection. Copy significant punctuation, model suffixes and units exactly where practicable.

If a translated label reads “large” while the source option ends in a numeric code, compare that code with the seller's size chart. The code could indicate a garment size, model year, capacity or pack count. Other sellers may use the same English word differently. Do not silently replace a code with an assumed meaning; state the exact selection and flag the attribute that still needs confirmation.
Separate the things you select together

Describe the independent selector dimensions. A shirt listing may use one row for colour, another for size and another for fit. A desk product might have separate selectors for width, finish and whether mounting hardware is included. Copying a single combined colour name without the other controls leaves an incomplete specification.

An example note for a shelf might say, “Selected finish shown as ash grey in the attached source text; width option 60 cm; mounting kit included; quantity one.” If the seller offers 60 centimetres as the inner usable width or as the total outside width, identify which one you need and request confirmation. The note should describe both what you clicked and what remains unknown. A technically precise number is of little use if it represents the wrong measurement.
Recheck the option after changing another selector

Some combinations depend on an earlier choice. Changing the finish may reset a size, replace the lead image or hide a bundle. After choosing the last field, reread all active options from the final summary. Save the screenshot at that point. A picture captured two screens earlier may show a combination that is no longer selected.

Suppose you initially choose a white double-layer pencil case and then switch to navy. The seller offers navy only in the single-layer version. If the interface resets the second selector, your final choice may be navy single-layer even though you remember tapping double-layer a minute earlier. Compare the displayed subtotal and option summary with the written requirements. If the exact combination cannot be reproduced, ask the seller what is available before submitting a manual request.
Distinguish similar labels with a comparison pair

When two options look alike, capture them side by side in your notes with their differences. One might show “with strap,” another “replacement strap.” A mistranslation that reduces both to “strap” could turn a bag purchase into an accessory purchase. Compare the unit, price difference, included pieces and seller option description before interpreting the intended selection.

For a real order, write down the rejected alternative as well as the chosen option if confusion is likely. A useful sentence is, “I want the complete green bag with shoulder strap. Do not select the spare shoulder strap offered under the same listing.” That instruction names the actual risk. A vague phrase such as “choose the correct version” leaves the purchaser with exactly the ambiguity you were trying to remove.
Match the confirmed order back to the source evidence

CNShopper's ordering guide asks buyers to provide size, colour, quantity and relevant seller notes before purchase. When a confirmation is available, compare its final option with the saved seller selection. Do this while a discrepancy can still be queried. If the confirmation abbreviates a long option, ask for clarification about the missing suffix or included component rather than accepting a generic matching title.

If a seller relists the same product under a new item number, treat the new page as a new offer. Keep the original record and compare both. Does the same option name still describe the same dimensions and pieces? Are the photographs reused from an earlier version? A note pasted from the old listing is a starting point for comparison. It does not establish that the new seller menu maps codes in the same way.
Use warehouse photos to test the requirement

At intake, ask which part of the option can actually be checked visually. Colour, printed size, visible construction and included pieces may be observable; material composition or long-term durability usually needs different evidence. A photograph of a closed box can show an option label without proving that every advertised component is inside. Frame your question around what a warehouse check can reasonably establish.

For the pencil case example, a straight-on exterior photograph might show navy but leave the number of layers unclear. Request a view of the open compartments tied to the correct warehouse entry, subject to the available service. Compare it against the confirmed order and your saved source selection. If the received unit is the single-layer option, the original wording and screenshot provide a much stronger explanation than a later claim that you remember selecting something else.
Keep an orderly record when the seller answers

If you receive clarification, save the seller's reply with its date and the specific listing. Record whether it confirms the existing option or proposes a substitute. For example, confirmation that “code C includes the mounting kit” is different from an offer to add the kit separately for an additional amount. Update the written specification if the proposed change is accepted.

Once the transaction is complete, retain the original option, the accepted summary and the evidence you used to approve the warehouse item. When you revisit the spreadsheet months later, you may see a different option order or different translations. Your record will still show what the seller offered at the time and what you actually commissioned. That is the practical value of keeping the seller's wording: it survives changes to the presentation long enough to answer questions about your particular purchase.

For matching pieces, check option consistency across more than one listing. A case and its separate strap can both be described as green while carrying different supplier color names or attachment widths. Ask for the precise label or measurement that connects the two. If a matching finish is essential, make that condition explicit before paying for either part. Two labels that translate into the same English word can still refer to separate finishes within the seller's own catalogue.
CNShopper order costs: separating seller postage from international freight

A shipping amount beside a Chinese marketplace product and a shipping amount displayed for an outbound parcel can both be correct. They cover different journeys. The first can pay the seller to get goods to the warehouse. The second can pay for movement from the warehouse toward your destination. Mixing them in one spreadsheet column makes a budget hard to check, especially when several purchases share a parcel.
Follow the goods rather than the word shipping

Draw the route in two parts. The merchant sends one or more units to the warehouse. Once goods are available and you have selected items for a parcel, the international delivery begins. CNShopper's ordering guide describes confirming product cost and domestic delivery before purchase, then reviewing the warehouse items and choosing international shipping. Use those distinct events as the basis of your purchasing record.

This does not imply that every seller charges domestic postage or that every checkout item has the same treatment. A seller may show delivery included, charge once for the order or change the amount according to the actual selection. Record precisely what the paid order shows. An empty shipping field on a catalogue card is an unknown input until you have verified how the live purchase handles it.
Use the seller order as the domestic accounting unit

Create one line for each seller order with the chosen goods subtotal, any domestic delivery charge and the transaction currency. If you want item-level detail, put the pieces beneath that seller order. Avoid automatically attaching the full domestic charge to each piece. Doing so counts the same movement several times.

Imagine seller A supplies two folders at 30 each and charges 8 to send both to the warehouse. The seller-order subtotal is 60 and the combined domestic cost is 68. Recording each folder as 30 plus 8 gives a total of 76 and overstates what was spent. You can allocate 4 of domestic cost to each folder for your internal analysis, but the seller charged 8 once. Keep the original invoice total alongside any optional allocation.
Add a second seller without changing the first invoice

Now suppose seller B supplies one binder at 50 plus 6 domestic delivery. The second purchase costs 56. Your combined purchase-stage cost for the three pieces is 124 in this illustrative example: 68 from seller A and 56 from seller B. Nothing about that sum identifies the price of the eventual international parcel. It is simply the cost of obtaining these items at the warehouse under the stated assumptions.

This separation becomes important when you later decide which goods should travel together. If you ship the binder first and the folders later, the original seller invoices stay the same. Your outbound parcel costs now belong to two parcel records. If all three pieces travel together, there is one outbound record to link to both seller purchases. The seller-to-warehouse history should not need to be rewritten each time you change a consolidation plan.
Keep estimates out of the paid column

At the planning stage you may want a freight allowance even before you have packed dimensions. Put that figure in an estimate field with its assumptions. Mark whether the input weight represents the item, retail packaging or proposed outbound box. Record the destination, route and date checked. When the packed quote arrives, retain the original assumption as a comparison rather than adding both figures as actual expenditure.

For example, your worksheet might contain an international allowance of 70 and later show an accepted quote of 82 in the same currency. Your freight budget moved by 12. You did not spend 152 merely because both figures appear in the file. If a separate optional service was purchased, give it its own field and determine whether the quote already includes it before adding it again.
Separate currency conversion from delivery changes

Keep the seller currency visible even when you prefer a home-currency budget. A catalogue conversion, the amount at purchase and the payment provider's posted charge may differ because they were calculated at different times or under different conversion rules. Compare source amounts in a common currency before attributing a difference to postage.

Consider an order where the seller invoice stays at 68 in the original currency but the converted estimate on a later visit changes. The domestic delivery line did not necessarily move. Check the original goods and postage lines first. If those are unchanged, review conversion and any distinct payment-provider charge separately. For a settled purchase, preserve the actual payment record rather than continuously recalculating what you historically paid from today's rate.
Allocate outbound freight only when it serves a decision

You may want to estimate the delivered cost of individual products. Decide which allocation rule matches your purpose and label it as your analysis. Equal division is easy when the pieces are similar. Dividing by item weight can be more informative for a dense binder and two light folders. Neither method automatically represents the carrier's true price per item; carriers typically quote the parcel as a whole under its service conditions.

Suppose the outbound example costs 90 and you allocate it equally across three pieces. Each receives an internal allocation of 30. If one rigid binder forces the box to be much larger, an equal split hides that fact. To investigate whether the binder should travel separately, compare real parcel scenarios with and without it. Arithmetic allocation explains how you divided an existing expense; a controlled quote comparison informs the separate decision about how to ship.
Handle changes, refunds and split fulfilment explicitly

If a merchant changes the quantity or issues a partial refund, update the seller purchase record with an adjustment. Keep the original payment and the adjustment as separate events. A return of one item does not automatically remove the entire domestic delivery charge from the original transaction. Check the actual amounts credited and any remaining service entries rather than reversing a charge because the goods count changed.

For a split seller shipment, keep the link between one seller invoice and multiple domestic carrier numbers. The existence of two labels does not prove that two domestic charges were paid by you. Conversely, two purchases from the same merchant need not share one delivery charge. Use the actual checkout and confirmed adjustments as your evidence. A transport event and a financial event are related, but their counts need not match.
Reconcile the budget when the parcel is ready

At dispatch, start with confirmed seller-order totals, then add the outbound freight and separate services once. Check the currency for each component and note which values are still estimates. If two figures disagree, ask which record they describe before asking why the amount changed. A mismatch frequently becomes understandable when you discover that one figure describes a single merchant and the other describes a mixed parcel.

A useful final note reads like a short explanation: “Two seller orders paid, three pieces received, one international parcel selected. Domestic delivery counted once on each invoice; packing and freight recorded against the parcel.” This gives you enough structure to investigate a price change without assigning it to the wrong party and to compare future purchases without forgetting the second journey.

A useful last check is to add the domestic charges at the same level at which they were quoted. If three lines share one seller shipment and the seller gave one combined figure, enter it once in the purchase total. If the account ultimately records separate domestic entries, reconcile those against the combined quote. Save the seller's explanation if different fulfillment locations or separate waybills changed how the goods were sent.
A size is unavailable on CNShopper: how to compare a substitute before agreeing

A selected size can disappear between saving a spreadsheet item and asking an agent to buy it. The useful response depends on what is missing: the seller may be out of stock, the imported selector may omit a valid option, or two sizing systems may be displayed differently. Establish which situation applies before accepting another size or telling the purchaser to cancel.
Recreate the exact combination

Return to the current seller listing. Select the intended colour, model or cut first, then inspect sizes for that combination. A medium available in a blue regular fit does not establish that a medium in a black short fit is available. Save the full original option text and the current view. Compare it with your earlier note and the order you submitted.

If the size appears on the seller page but is missing from the imported purchase screen, report the discrepancy with the seller link and two clear screenshots. Ask whether the exact option can be confirmed. If it is absent from both screens, ask the merchant about availability through the appropriate channel. A seller estimate for a future restock is different from a confirmed unit available for purchase now. Record which kind of answer you received.
Identify the fit requirement behind the label

A label such as M or EU 42 is a shorthand; it does not describe every relevant dimension. Determine what made the original size attractive. For trousers, you might need a particular waist range, rise, thigh width and inseam. For a shirt, chest width, shoulder position, sleeve length and overall length may matter independently. Write down the limiting measurement rather than assuming one size up or down will work.

Choose a comparison garment with a similar construction that fits for the same use. A loose sweatshirt for layering and a tailored jacket worn over a shirt do not serve as interchangeable baselines. Lay the comparison garment as the seller's diagram instructs and record units and endpoints. A waist circumference on a size table cannot be compared directly to a relaxed flat width without checking how both were measured.
Confirm what the proposed alternative actually is

Ask for the exact seller option, not just the translated words “similar size.” A proposed replacement might be the next size of the same garment, the same label in another cut, a different colour that remains in stock or a different listing entirely. Each requires a different comparison. If the seller offers a substitute from another listing, obtain its own chart, photos, price and conditions.

Imagine a jacket unavailable in short medium. The alternatives are regular medium and short large. Regular medium may keep a similar chest width while adding body length. Short large may retain the intended length while increasing width and shoulder span. Neither is universally “closer.” State which dimensions you need to preserve and compare both alternatives with those requirements. If the necessary measurements are absent, the correct conclusion is uncertainty rather than a confident size recommendation.
Read size charts as measurements, not conversion tables

Look for the measurement method, units, garment position and whether the numbers describe the item or the wearer. A body chart showing recommended chest circumference has a different meaning from the actual finished garment circumference. An elastic waistband measured flat and relaxed can differ substantially from its stretched width. Ask for clarification when a term such as “waist” appears without a diagram.

For an illustrative example, your own jacket measures 54 centimetres flat underarm to underarm. A seller chart lists chest 108. The figures might describe similar garment widths if 108 is the complete garment circumference using comparable endpoints. They are not necessarily equivalent if 108 is a recommended wearer measurement. This arithmetic only identifies the question to ask. It does not prove that the substitute will fit, because cut, sleeve shape and fabric behaviour can also differ.
Decide whether a measurement could change your answer

If the seller can provide a measurement before purchase, identify the one or two details that would resolve the uncertainty. “What are all the dimensions?” may generate another generic chart. “For the short large in black, what is the centre-back length from collar seam to hem?” identifies an exact option and measurement. Ask whether the current stock is the version represented by the chart.

If the only available measurement comes after warehouse intake, decide whether the purchase risk and current return conditions are acceptable before ordering. CNShopper describes warehouse photographs as a visual review and notes that additional inspection can depend on availability. An expectation that later photos will answer your question is not the same as a confirmed seller commitment to supply a suitable size or accept a return.
Give the purchaser an explicit decision

Once you choose, send an instruction that names the original order and the precise action. If you accept the substitute, specify the replacement seller option, quantity, confirmed price and any required condition. If you decline it, say whether you want the order held for clarification or cancelled according to the options actually available. Avoid mixing “try the large” with “only buy medium” in the same message.

For example, “The requested black short M is unavailable. Please order black short L only if the seller confirms the back length at the agreed measurement. If it exceeds that figure, contact me before purchase.” If you do not want a conditional purchase, use a simpler decision and wait for the answer first. Keep the purchaser's confirmation alongside your message so it is clear which instruction was accepted.
Compare the warehouse item with the revised order

At intake, review the accepted replacement specification, not merely the first item saved to your spreadsheet. If you approved short large, a large label can be correct even though the original wishlist said medium. However, the label alone may not confirm the cut or measurement that justified the change. Request the appropriate view for the remaining question if the service permits it.

Keep the photo linked to the specific order. Two black jackets photographed on the same surface can be easy to confuse. Look for the option label, an overall view and the relevant measurement. If the received item differs from the revised confirmation, describe that exact difference to support while the unit is available for inspection. The original request and the accepted substitution provide the context for the discrepancy.
Preserve the original outcome for future purchases

Save a short result such as “short medium unavailable; accepted short large after checking back length; actual warehouse measurement recorded.” If you declined a substitute, keep the reason, such as excessive length or incompatible rise. Those notes improve future purchases from the same seller without pretending that a size label has universal meaning across shops.

The decision is complete when you can identify the actual available option, explain why its measurements do or do not meet your need and point to the instruction the purchaser received. A different size can be reasonable, but its suitability should follow from the garment and the use you have in mind. It should never depend solely on a familiar letter, a similar thumbnail or a hurried suggestion to choose the next option.

Keep a record of the option you declined as well as the one you approved. If a seller offers both a different color in the requested size and the requested color in a different size, a reply referring to the “second option” can become unclear when messages are translated or forwarded. Repeat the accepted color, size and model in full, and request confirmation on the affected purchase line.
How to write a CNShopper after-sales request that identifies the problem

An effective after-sales request lets another person reconstruct the purchase, see what went wrong and understand what decision you need. The evidence changes depending on whether the goods are with the seller, in the agent's warehouse or already at your address. CNShopper's ordering and help pages give context for those stages. Check the options available on your own order before asking for a remedy. Availability, timing and costs can depend on the seller, service and circumstances.
Identify the exact purchase line

Open the original order and copy the product title, seller option text, quantity and line reference. Include the warehouse or international parcel reference if the problem happened later. A single shipment can contain several nearly identical products. If you report that “the black one is wrong,” the agent has to guess which seller or purchase you mean. Spell out the distinguishing detail in the first sentence, such as the black single-pocket organizer from the particular purchase line you identify.

Explain the agreed specification using the record from the time of purchase. Sellers can change photographs and option names on a live page. A saved selection, confirmation message or dated screenshot can show the original wording. If you supplied special instructions, include the agent's response along with your own message. A request to choose the longer model and an acknowledgement that the seller could supply it are two different pieces of evidence. Keep their roles clear.
Describe one observable discrepancy

State what you expected, what you can see and where the observation came from. “The selected option says two inner pockets. The inside photograph of this warehouse item shows one stitched pocket” gives the agent something to inspect. “Bad quality” could mean an appearance issue, incorrect material, poor workmanship or a damaged shipment. When the difference cannot be seen in a photo, describe the practical symptom and the conditions under which you observed it.

A fit concern needs different evidence from a wrong-size shipment. Check the sewn-in label and how the seller defines the listed measurements. A garment that feels tight can carry the exact ordered size. If a seller gave a garment width, show which two points you measured and whether the fabric was stretched. If you only have a size label, report that observation honestly. Ask whether another measurement or photograph is available if it would help establish the distinction.
Choose photographs that can answer a question

Use an overall image to orient the person reviewing the case, then add a closer image of the disputed detail. For a color mismatch, photograph both the product and any option label if they are available. Describe the lighting when color is central to the decision. Screen settings, warehouse lighting and the original listing image can all affect appearance. A label with the seller's color code can give the reviewer a second way to identify what was sent.

For a damaged delivery, keep the packaging while the issue is being assessed. Photograph the outside condition and the item's location or protective material if you can do so at the time of opening. Describe what you directly observed. A crushed corner on a box and a scratch on the goods can both be documented without deciding who caused the damage. If you noticed the scratch later, say when you found it. That detail helps the reviewer interpret the evidence fairly.
Match the request to the item's location

If the item is still in the warehouse, decide whether you want more information before an exchange or return. The issue may be resolved by a clearer image of a label or a count of pieces inside a bundle. Specify the warehouse item and ask whether the check involves opening sealed packaging or paying a fee. Keep it out of a parcel submission while you are deciding. Once the item is packed with unrelated goods, identifying and separating it may require a different process.

If you already received the item overseas, describe the delivery and opening dates as accurately as possible. Read the service information attached to the parcel and ask where to submit the relevant documents. Do not send an unrequested international return to an address copied from a domestic label. Ask for the authorized recipient, required reference, method and who would pay each leg before arranging any shipment. Keep written instructions together with the case so future tracking can be matched to the correct request.
Ask for a specific remedy and its conditions

Choose the practical result you need. An additional inspection, exchange for a named option, return assessment or clarification of a charge each requires a different response. When requesting an exchange, specify what to do if the replacement is unavailable. A second-choice color you mentioned casually earlier can be mistaken for authorization. Give a clear instruction to pause if a replacement would change the size, design, price or another feature that affects your decision.

If money is involved, ask for the amount, currency and components before agreeing. A seller refund, domestic return postage, a service fee and international freight may appear in different records. Ask which amounts the proposed resolution addresses and where a credit would appear. When comparing the proposal with your original payment, use the affected line. A payment that covered several products is an unreliable measure of the cost associated with a single defective item.
Put the evidence in an order the reviewer can follow

Start with your request, then identify the item and give a short sequence of events. For example, explain that you ordered a particular organizer, a warehouse photo shows a different fastening, and you would like the agent to check the seller option before international packing. Follow with the purchase reference, the original option wording and two labeled images. The reviewer can now inspect the records in the same order you used to identify the issue.

Attach private identifying information only through the official support channel when necessary. A parcel reference and purchase line often provide a cleaner starting point than a full screenshot of your account, balance and delivery address. Keep originals of images that you crop for a message. If support requests a wider view of the package or the complete label, you can share the requested version through the appropriate channel without losing your original context.
Record the response and check that it was carried out

Save the date and wording of a proposed resolution before approving it. If an exchange is offered, verify whether the proposal covers the return to the seller, the replacement purchase and its delivery back to the warehouse. If clarification is still needed, reply within the existing case when possible and list the one point preventing a decision. Repeating the initial complaint in a new thread can separate useful photographs from the answer they prompted.

Finally, compare the actual result with what you approved. For an exchange, inspect the new warehouse entry against the corrected option. For a refund, find the associated transaction and check its amount and currency against the agreement. For a shipping claim, keep the parcel reference with the final message. Close your notes with what happened and what remains outstanding. That final comparison catches cases where a seller accepted a return but the replacement or credit still needs to be identified.

If several identical units were purchased, specify which units the outcome covers. A credit offered for one damaged piece does not settle a separate quantity discrepancy on the same purchase. Keep one line per issue in your notes, even if support handles both in a single case. That small distinction makes the final comparison with the agent's response much easier.
Writing a manual purchase specification a CNShopper buyer can actually use

A useful manual purchase specification answers a practical question: could someone who has never seen your spreadsheet order the correct unit from the correct seller using only your message? If the answer depends on recognizing a familiar image, improve the specification before sending it. A short, unambiguous instruction is more effective than several paragraphs of preferences that contradict the selected option.
Name the item in a way that survives translation

Start with the seller's product URL and the exact original option wording. Add a plain-language description in your own language. These fields serve different functions. The original wording helps the purchaser select the right seller control. Your explanation tells the purchaser why the choice matters. One should not silently replace the other.

Imagine a listing for a lunchbox in which the options translate as “standard,” “enhanced” and “portable.” The word “portable” sounds as though it could describe every lunchbox. The seller's original option may identify a specific two-tier version with a carrying handle. Record the original text, a screenshot of the selection and a description such as “two stackable compartments with handle.” If the seller page and your interpretation disagree, ask the question before commissioning the purchase.
Specify the unit before the quantity

Define what counts as one ordered unit. A stationery listing may sell one pencil, one pack of twelve or one display box of packs. The photograph can depict all three at once. A quantity of two means very different things depending on which selector is active. Write the selected unit alongside the desired number and the expected physical total.
